payload.text: Explain token caching in about 100 words. Use no tools.

data.text: Token caching stores previously computed tokens so repeated requests can reuse them instead of processing the same context again. In AI systems, this often means caching a prompt’s unchanged prefix—such as system instructions or conversation history—while generating only the new portion. Caching can reduce latency, computation, and cost, especially for long prompts used repeatedly. Cached data may expire, be evicted when storage is full, or become invalid when the underlying content or model changes. It is most effective when requests share substantial, stable input. Sensitive cached content should also be protected, since it may contain private instructions or user data.

payload.text: Give one example of token caching paying off, in about 100 words. Use no tools.

data.text: A customer-support assistant receives thousands of requests each day using the same 5,000-token policy manual, safety rules, and company procedures. Without caching, the system repeatedly processes that entire shared prefix for every conversation. With token caching, the provider stores the processed representation of the unchanged instructions. Each new request only adds the customer’s question and relevant conversation, reducing processing time and input cost. The benefit grows as the shared prefix gets longer and is reused more frequently. If the company updates its policy manual, however, the cached version must expire or be invalidated so the assistant follows the latest rules.
